title: At a Restaurant
levelNote: Six tiers in one file. A beginner orders a simple meal and asks for the bill; an advanced learner handles a reservation, a substitution, and a polite complaint — same topic, same file, different depth.

reading.title: A family meal out
reading.text:
On Saturday, the Costa family went to a small restaurant near the beach. The waiter showed them to a table by the window and gave them the menu.

The children ordered pizza, and their parents chose fish with rice. Everyone was hungry, so the food did not stay on the plates for long.

At the end, their father asked for the bill and left a small tip for the friendly waiter. They all agreed it was a wonderful evening.

questions.q: What did the father do at the end?

reading.title: A memorable restaurant experience
reading.text:
Marco still remembers the first time he ate at a proper restaurant instead of a fast food place. He was nervous about which fork to use and whether he was supposed to order a starter, so he watched what everyone else at the table did before choosing anything himself.

When the food arrived, he realized his worry had been unnecessary. The waiter was patient, happy to explain what was in each dish, and did not mind at all when Marco asked for the sauce on the side because he was not used to spicy food.

What he remembers most, though, is not the meal itself but how relaxed the evening became once he stopped worrying about doing everything correctly. Good service, he decided, is less about rules and more about making a nervous guest feel comfortable.

questions.q: Why was Marco nervous at first?
options: He did not know the restaurant rules
He did not like the food

questions.q: How did the waiter help him?
options: By seating him near the kitchen

questions.q: What does Marco conclude about good service?
options: It is about following strict rules
It is about serving food quickly
It is about making guests comfortable

reading.title: The etiquette of tipping
reading.text:
Tipping is one of the strangest customs in the restaurant world, mostly because nobody agrees on it. In some countries a tip is expected and its absence is read as an insult; in others, offering one can seem to suggest the waiter was not already paid a fair wage. Visitors are left guessing, usually by watching what the table next to them does.

The confusion is not really about money. A tip left after a good meal is a small, specific thank you: it says the service itself, not just the food, made the evening better. Removing that signal does not remove the feeling behind it, which is probably why the custom survives even in places that keep trying to simplify it with an automatic service charge.

What makes a restaurant experience good rarely appears on the receipt. It is the waiter who remembers you do not like ice in your water, the kitchen that quietly adjusts a dish for an allergy, the quiet at a table that lets a conversation actually happen. The food matters, obviously. It is just not the whole evening.

questions.q: According to the text, why is tipping confusing for visitors?
options: It is always included automatically everywhere

questions.q: What does the writer say a tip actually communicates?
options: That the restaurant needs more customers
That the service made the evening better

questions.q: What does the writer suggest makes a restaurant experience good?
options: More than just the food itself
Only the price of the meal

speaking.text: Have you ever tried the seafood here?

speaking.text: I have been waiting for twenty minutes.

speaking.text: I'm sorry, but this isn't what I ordered.
speaking.tip: Isn't is one quick syllable: IZ-nt.

speaking.text: Could you take this back to the kitchen?

speaking.text: The service charge is already included, isn't it?
speaking.tip: Your voice rises slightly on isn't it, since you expect the answer is yes.
